title: US-China: The AI rivalry that surpasses summitry
author: Jack Sato
text: |United States, explained.Export controls are one of the key tools the United States has used to protect its lead in AI (Saradasish Pradhan/Unsplash)US-China: The AI rivalry that surpasses summitryThe upcoming Xi-Trump meeting on the sidelines of the APEC meeting shouldn’t distract from the fierce AI competition underway.Jack Sato17 November 20263 min read|US-China: The AI rivalry that surpasses summitryUS-China: The AI rivalry that surpasses summitryWhen Donald Trump and Xi Jinping meet on the sidelines of the APEC summit later this week, AI will be high on the agenda. US Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent has signalled that Washington wants to use the talks to advance a new bilateral dialogue on AI (Opens in new window). Yet he also warned that both sides should “harbour no illusions” about their differences – they remain rivals in the race for AI.However the APEC summit talks go, Washington will need to remain vigilant to stay ahead.A recent Lowy Institute paper – Asia Power Snapshot: China, the United States, and the race for AI dominance (Opens in new window) – found that the United States holds a clear lead in the capabilities of its frontier models, driven by its dominance in computing power. To guard that advantage, Washington has sought to limit China’s access to the most advanced technologies. Whatever comes out of the summit, Beijing will continue to seek ways to bypass those restrictions.Former Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang, who recently resigned after admitting (Opens in new window) to an affair, has renewed attention on Chinese efforts to get around US restrictions. The woman involved is reportedly a former Megaspeed executive. Megaspeed is one of Nvidia’s biggest foreign customers, and according to The New York Times (Opens in new window), US officials concluded she was a Chinese intelligence asset, a claim Beijing rejects (Opens in new window). Megaspeed has faced scrutiny (Opens in new window) over alleged export violations, which it denies (Opens in new window).ResearchAsia Power Snapshot: China, the United States, and the race for AI dominanceRead data snapshotObservers have long suspected that smugglers route advanced chips to China through Southeast Asia. In March 2026, US prosecutors charged a co-founder of Super Micro (Opens in new window), a server maker, with conspiring to divert servers containing Nvidia chips. Prosecutors alleged that the scheme sent roughly US$2.5 billion worth of AI technology to China. In October 2026, Malaysian customs seized servers containing about US$12 million worth of AI chips (Opens in new window) at Kuala Lumpur’s international airport.China has also looked to outsource its computation abroad. The New York Times reported (Opens in new window) that Megaspeed has used Nvidia chips in data centres across Malaysia and Indonesia that appear to serve China. INF Tech, a Chinese AI startup, has accessed restricted chips (Opens in new window) by renting them from an Indonesian firm.Washington has tried to plug some of these gaps. It has pressured Southeast Asian countries such as Malaysia to tighten their regulations (Opens in new window), and Congress is advancing legislation to close loopholes. In January 2026, the US House of Representatives passed the Remote Access Security Act (Opens in new window), which would extend export controls to cloud-based access to restricted chips. The Senate is yet to vote on it. In March, a House committee passed the Chip Security Act (Opens in new window), which would require advanced chips to carry on-chip mechanisms that would verify their location and detect tampering. Complementing these, in May 2026, the US Department of Commerce moved to block sales of advanced chips to subsidiaries (Opens in new window) of Chinese companies based outside China.Shenzhen, host city for the upcoming Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation summit, in China's southern Guangdong province (Greg Baker/Getty Images)However, some of these measures have met resistance. The Semiconductor Industry Association, which represents chipmakers such as Nvidia, has opposed the Chip Security Act (Opens in new window), saying that it cannot support “blanket mandates” for on-chip mechanisms it argues are untested and potentially infeasible.Even if these bills pass, controls alone may not be sufficient, as Chinese firms have also sought to innovate their way around them.One barrier Chinese companies have tried to overcome is their lack of access to advanced lithography equipment. Dutch company ASML, which makes these machines, has curbed sales to China under pressure from Washington (Opens in new window). They are necessary for shrinking transistors, a key component of semiconductors. Adding more transistors to a chip increases its processing speed and, by extension, its computing power. In May 2026, Huawei announced a new chip-design approach (Opens in new window) that aims to increase transistor density without shrinking transistors. It hopes to match, by 2031, the transistor density of the chips Taiwan’s TSMC plans to produce in 2028 (Opens in new window) – potentially without the need for the advanced lithography machines Chinese firms struggle to obtain.Export controls are one of the key tools the United States has used to protect its lead in AI. But Chinese firms have repeatedly sought ways to bypass them, whether through third countries or new chip designs. However the APEC summit talks go, Washington will need to remain vigilant to stay ahead.About the authorJack SatoJack Sato is a Data Analyst for the Asia Power Index at the Lowy Institute.
